teaser.text: Whitbread is a hotel company whose main business is selling dependable places to sleep, principally through Premier Inn. Its money comes mainly from rooms, with food, drink and optional services adding value around the stay.

blocks.heading: Where could Whitbread's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast reaches 2,685.24p in October 2027, with the outcome hinging on cash conversion, room returns and Germany’s progress. It reaches 3,647.69p in October 2029.

The October 2027 weighted price implies a 7% total return from today. The October 2029 weighted price implies a 51% total return. The bear case carries 30%. The base case carries 50%, and the bull case 20%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Whitbread's forecast?

paragraphs.text: EBITDA is the central operating judgement. The base case starts at £1,090m. It reaches £1,150m in October 2028 and £1,210m in October 2029, against FY26 adjusted EBITDA of £1,075.1m. Bear EBITDA falls to £995m in 2028; bull EBITDA reaches £1,350m by 2029. Recent accommodation sales rose 3% and RevPAR rose 2%, while management guides to £60m of efficiencies and substantial room openings.

The bear case gives cost inflation, business rates and the restaurant transition more weight. Business-rate costs add £35m, while the transition reduces adjusted PBT by £40m. The bull case assumes efficiencies, room openings and German maturation overcome those pressures. Germany’s £8m segment loss, despite £22m of mature-cohort site profit, explains why the upside is not central.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Whitbread really make?

paragraphs.text: Capital spending was £675.4m. Lease principal payments were £172.9m. Together they turned operating cash into free cash flow of negative £95.5m. Subtracting £16.7m of share-based pay gives analytical “real” free cash flow of negative £112.2m, because shares still transfer value to employees even without immediate cash leaving.

dividend.title: Whitbread dividend: payment and cash cover
dividend.meta_description: Whitbread paid 97.00p per share, but its free cash flow was negative £95.5m.
dividend.opening: Whitbread paid 97.00p per share in FY26, but its FY26 free cash flow was negative £95.5m, so the dividend was not covered by that year's free cash flow. The latest forecast keeps the base dividend at £0.97, although that payout remains an assumption while cash conversion improves.
dividend.closing: The full memo also covers Whitbread’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Whitbread pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The effective tax rate was 28.7%. Diluted EPS fell less than net income because the share count declined, while the dividend stayed at 97.00p. Shareholders therefore received a larger portion of statutory earnings.

The base dividend holds at £0.97 because that payout has remained unchanged through FY24–FY26 and the latest interim dividend was 36.40p. The bear case cuts it to £0.40 as negative free cash flow persists; the bull case reaches £1.12 as cash conversion improves. FY26 free cash flow was negative £95.5m, which makes the base case an assumption rather than a certainty.

blocks.heading: Is Whitbread’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Capital spending was £675.4m. Lease principal payments were £172.9m. Together they turned operating cash into free cash flow of negative £95.5m. Subtracting £16.7m of share-based pay gives analytical “real” free cash flow of negative £112.2m, because shares still transfer value to employees even without immediate cash leaving.

Investment and distributions compete for the same cash. FY26 free cash flow was negative £95.5m, while the latest half-year produced £54.2m. Shareholder distributions were approximately £102m in that half-year. Property sales and deferred projects can help, but maintenance, rent and refinancing cannot be removed as freely as a buyback.

paragraphs.text: Management targets a 500-basis-point increase in Group ROCE by FY31. It also targets £2bn available for dividends and buybacks. Growth capex must earn at least a 15% return, with FY27 net capex guidance of £200m–£300m.
